newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Police, troops, tanks patrol Colombian riot town.
newsitem.headline: Police, troops, tanks patrol Colombian riot town.

text.p: Hundreds of soldiers and riot police backed by light tanks patroled this town on the outskirts of Bogota on Wednesday after violent protests against recent public service price hikes.

Red Cross spokesmen said at least one person was killed and more than 20 injured in all-night clashes on Tuesday with security forces. During the fighting, which the authorities said were stirred by leftist guerrillas, protesters armed with firebombs and rocks battled riot police.
The protester killed died of a gunshot wound to the head, the Red Cross said. Facatativa is a working-class community 18 miles (30 km) west of the capital.

The fighting broke out after police moved in to clear barricades halting transportation since Monday along a key highway linking the capital to the northwest industrial hub of Medellin and the Atlantic coast.

The protesters went on an all-night rampage after police cleared the barricades, setting fire to the mayor's office and looting or ransacking at least 28 stores and banks throughout the centre of the town of about 20,000 people.

By Wednesday afternoon, more than 500 police and troops took control of the town's main square while about 2,000 demonstrators taunted them from side streets. At least four light tanks drove through the protest-scarred streets and shops remained closed. No fresh clashes were reported during the afternoon.

National Police chief Gen. Rosso Jose Serrano accused leftist rebels of fuelling the disturbances, saying: "A movement of this magnitude does not occur spontaneously. The guerrillas must be taking advantage of this."
Earlier in the day, Defence Minister Juan Carlos Esguerra said the townspeople were being used by "people interested in disorder, in chaos and in sowing anarchy."
Guerrillas are known to operate out of rural areas near Facatativa but a police spokeswoman said there was no evidence to point toward their direct involvement in the protests.

Protesters interviewed by Reuter Television in Facatativa early on Wednesday said their main demand was for a cut in electricity rates, which recently increased in the area by as much as 300 percent. Water prices have undergone similar increases as the government moves to slash public service subsidies, the demontrators said.
"This is about the injustice of the government," said one protester, who identified himself only as a university student.

He said police themselves had been responsible for much of the damage in the centre of Facatativa, saying they had used their trucheons to smash windows throughout the area and had also fired tear gas into people's homes.
